prompt: Oxygen's ground-state configuration is 1s^2 2s^2 2p_x^2 2p_y^1 2p_z^1. Without hybridization, which oxygen orbitals would form the two O–H bonds?

choices.text: The half-filled 2p_y and 2p_z orbitals
The completely filled 2s and 2p_x orbitals
choices.why: Filled orbitals already hold an electron pair. The bonds use the singly occupied 2p_y and 2p_z, each pairing with an H 1s electron.

choices.text: The 2s orbital and the half-filled 2p_z
choices.why: 2s is filled, so it holds a lone pair here. The two unfilled orbitals are 2p_y and 2p_z.

choices.text: The 1s core and the filled 2s orbitals
choices.why: These are filled, and 1s is a core orbital. The bonding orbitals are the unfilled 2p_y and 2p_z.

explanation: Only 2p_y and 2p_z are unfilled, each with one electron, so each can pair with an H 1s electron. The bonding wavefunctions then mix |2p_y⟩ or |2p_z⟩ on O with |1s⟩ on one H atom.

prompt: Why does the hydrogen 1s orbital play no part in setting the direction of an O–H bond in water?

choices.text: It is spherical, with no preferred direction
It is too small to overlap with oxygen orbitals
choices.why: The 1s orbital does overlap with an O orbital to form the bond. It just has no direction of its own, so the O orbitals set the bond direction.

choices.text: It is filled, so it takes no part in bonding
choices.why: Atomic H is 1s^1, with a single electron that pairs with an O electron in the bond. It sets no direction because it is spherical.

choices.text: It has a node that cancels out its direction
choices.why: A 1s orbital has no nodes. It has no preferred direction simply because it is spherical.

explanation: Atomic hydrogen is 1s^1, a spherical orbital with no preferred orientation. So the shape of water must come from the oxygen orbitals used in the bonds.

prompt: If oxygen used only its 2p_y and 2p_z orbitals to bond to the two H atoms, what H–O–H angle would be expected?

choices.text: 90°, since 2p_y and 2p_z are perpendicular
109.5°, since oxygen has four electron groups
choices.why: 109.5° comes from four sp^3 hybrids. Pure 2p_y and 2p_z orbitals lie along the y and z axes, at 90° to each other.

choices.text: 180°, since the two H atoms repel each other
choices.why: Bonds made from pure p orbitals are fixed along the y and z axes, so the angle would be 90°.

choices.text: 104.45°, the experimental value for water
choices.why: That is what is measured, and it is exactly why pure p orbitals are a poor model: they predict 90°.

explanation: 2p_y and 2p_z are oriented at 90° to each other, so bonds made from them would meet at 90°. The measured angle, 104.45°, shows that using the atomic orbitals directly is not a good model.

prompt: What is the experimentally measured H–O–H bond angle of water?

choices.why: That is the ideal angle for four sp^3 hybrids. Water's measured angle is a little smaller, 104.45°.
That is what bonds from pure 2p_y and 2p_z orbitals would give. Experiment finds 104.45°.
That is the angle between sp^2 hybrids. Experiment finds 104.45° for water.

explanation: Experiment gives 104.45°, with an O–H bond length of 0.9584 Å, in agreement with VSEPR theory. It lies between the 90° of pure p orbitals and the 109.5° of perfect sp^3 hybrids.

prompt: Why can mixing some 2s character into oxygen's 2p orbitals change the predicted bond angle of water?

choices.text: It creates hybrids that point off the p axes
It adds electrons that push the H atoms apart
choices.why: Mixing orbitals doesn't add electrons. Because 2s is spherical, mixing it in creates hybrids whose directions are no longer fixed along the axes.

choices.text: It makes oxygen's 2p orbitals spherical too
choices.why: Only some 2s is mixed in, so the hybrids keep a direction; it is just no longer along an x, y or z axis.

choices.text: It lowers the energy of the H 1s orbitals
choices.why: The H orbitals are unchanged. It is the O orbitals whose directions change when 2s character is mixed in.

explanation: The 2s orbital is spherical, so mixing some of it into the p orbitals creates new hybrid orbitals whose directions differ from the p axes. That lets the bond angle move away from 90°.

prompt: How does the section rate valence bond theory's historical success at explaining bond angles in small molecules?

choices.text: It was only qualitatively correct
It predicted every angle exactly
choices.why: The section says VB was only qualitatively correct; for water, simple hybrids don't give 104.45° without adjusting their s and p character.

choices.text: It failed to explain any bond angle
choices.why: VB did explain bond angles, such as the bend of water, but only qualitatively.

choices.text: It worked only for linear molecules
choices.why: VB was used for bent molecules too, such as water. It was qualitatively, not quantitatively, correct.

explanation: Historically, valence bond theory was used to explain bond angles in small molecules, but it was only qualitatively correct. Water shows this: perfect sp^3 hybrids give 109.5°, not the measured 104.45°.

prompt: When oxygen's 2s and three 2p orbitals form four sp^3 hybrids in water, how are its six valence electrons placed in them?

choices.text: Two half filled for bonds, two filled as lone pairs
All four half filled, so oxygen could form four bonds
choices.why: Four half-filled hybrids hold only 4 electrons. O has 6 valence electrons: 1 + 1 in the bonding hybrids and 2 + 2 in the lone pairs.

choices.text: Three filled with lone pairs and one left empty
choices.why: That puts all 6 electrons in lone pairs and leaves nothing to bond with the two H atoms.

choices.text: One and a half electrons in each of the four
choices.why: An orbital holds a whole number of electrons: 0, 1 or 2. Two hybrids are half filled and two are completely filled.

explanation: Of the four sp^3 hybrids, two are half filled and pair with the H 1s electrons to form the O–H bonds, and the other two are completely filled and hold the two lone pairs: 1 + 1 + 2 + 2 = 6 electrons.

prompt: Four electron groups around an atom ideally meet at 109.5°, yet water's angle is 104.45°. What is the VSEPR explanation?

choices.text: Lone pairs take up more space and push the bonds together
Bonding pairs take up more space than lone pairs
choices.why: It's the other way round: lone pairs take up more volume, so their repulsion with the bonding pairs squeezes the H–O–H angle.

choices.text: The hydrogen atoms attract each other across the molecule
choices.why: VSEPR is about repulsion between electron pairs. The bulkier lone pairs repel the bonding pairs more strongly.

choices.text: Oxygen has only three electron groups, not four
choices.why: Oxygen has four groups: two bonding pairs and two lone pairs. The lone pairs' greater repulsion makes the angle smaller than 109.5°.

explanation: Lone pairs take up more volume than bonding pairs, so lone pair–bonding pair repulsions are greater. They push the O–H bonds closer together, making the H–O–H angle smaller than the ideal 109.5°.

prompt: Why can't the four hybrids on oxygen in water all be perfect sp^3 hybrids?

choices.text: Its bond angle isn't the sp^3 angle, 109.5°
Oxygen has no 2s orbital that could be mixed in
choices.why: Oxygen does have a 2s orbital, and it is mixed in. The problem is that perfect sp^3 hybrids meet at 109.5°, not 104.45°.

choices.text: Hybrids in a molecule must be pure p orbitals
choices.why: Hybrids are mixtures of s and p by definition. Water's are not perfect sp^3 because its angle isn't 109.5°.

choices.text: Oxygen has more than three 2p orbitals
choices.why: Oxygen has exactly three 2p orbitals. The issue is that a 104.45° angle doesn't match the 109.5° of perfect sp^3 hybrids.

explanation: Perfect sp^3 hybrids are 25% s and 75% p and meet at 109.5°. Since water's angle is 104.45°, its hybrids can't have exactly this mix; the s and p character is spread unevenly over the four hybrids.

prompt: What does the hybrid label sp^(x) stand for?

choices.text: A hybrid that is 1/(x + 1) s and x/(x + 1) p
One s orbital mixed with x whole p orbitals
choices.why: x needn't count whole p orbitals; water's sp^4 hybrids don't contain four p orbitals. The label gives fractions: s = 1/(x + 1), p = x/(x + 1).

choices.text: A set of x hybrids made from one s orbital
choices.why: x doesn't count hybrids; four sp^3 hybrids come from one s and three p orbitals. It sets the p-to-s ratio.

choices.text: A hybrid that is x% s and the rest p
choices.why: x isn't a percentage. The s fraction is 1/(x + 1), for example 1/4 = 25% for sp^3.

explanation: The label is an abbreviation: an sp^(x) hybrid has s fraction 1/(x + 1) and p fraction x/(x + 1). For sp^3 that is 1/4 s and 3/4 p, and in principle x can take any value.

prompt: An sp^(x) hybrid has s fraction 1/(x + 1). One of the valid schemes listed in the section includes an sp^(2/3) hybrid, with x = 2/3. What is its s character, in %?
explanation: 1/(x + 1) = 1/(2/3 + 1) = 1/(5/3) = 3/5 = 60%. x need not be a whole number, and with x below 1 the hybrid has more s than p character.

prompt: If one s orbital and three p orbitals are used to make three sp^2 hybrids, what else is left?

choices.text: One unhybridized p orbital
One unhybridized s orbital
choices.why: The single s orbital is used up in the three sp^2 hybrids, so a p orbital is what's left over.

choices.text: Nothing; all four orbitals become sp^2
choices.why: Four orbitals always give four orbitals. Three sp^2 hybrids use the s and two of the p orbitals, leaving one p.

choices.text: Two unhybridized p orbitals
choices.why: Each sp^2 hybrid is 1/3 s and 2/3 p, so three of them use two p orbitals in all, leaving just one of the three.

explanation: The number of orbitals is kept: 1 × s and 3 × p make 4 orbitals. Three sp^2 hybrids use the s and two p orbitals, so the scheme is 3 × sp^2 + 1 × p.

prompt: One s and three p orbitals could give 4 × sp^3, or 3 × sp^2 + 1 × p, or many other sets. According to the section, what decides which set is valid for a molecule?

choices.text: Only experiment, such as structure or spectroscopy
Always the set with the most hybrids, 4 × sp^3
choices.why: 4 × sp^3 is just one of virtually infinite possibilities. Water shows that it isn't automatically right.

choices.text: The number of electrons on the central atom alone
choices.why: Electron counting doesn't settle it. Only experiment, such as the molecular structure or spectroscopy, tells which description is valid.

choices.text: Whichever set makes the arithmetic simplest
choices.why: Convenience doesn't decide. Only experiment, such as structure or spectroscopy, determines which scheme is valid.

explanation: There are virtually infinite ways to combine one s and three p orbitals. Which combination is valid is determined only by experiment, for example the molecule's structure or its spectroscopy.

prompt: A general hybrid is written |χ_i⟩ = N(p + γs). What does γ describe?

choices.text: The relative amount of s mixed into the hybrid
The normalization constant of the hybrid
choices.why: That is N, which equals 1/√(1 + γ^2). γ is the relative contribution of s character.

choices.text: The bond angle between two of the hybrids
choices.why: γ is related to the angle through cos θ = −γ^2, but γ itself is the s mixing coefficient.

choices.text: The number of p orbitals used to build the hybrid
choices.why: γ is a coefficient, not a count. γ = 0 means a pure p orbital, and larger γ means more s character.

explanation: N normalizes the hybrid, and γ is the relative contribution of s character. γ = 0 gives a pure p orbital, γ = 1/√3 a pure sp^3 hybrid and γ = 1 a pure sp hybrid.

prompt: When the hybrid N(p + γs) is normalized, why does the cross term containing the integral ∫sp dτ drop out?

choices.text: The s and p orbitals are orthogonal
The s and p orbitals are each normalized
choices.why: Normalization makes ∫p^2 dτ and ∫s^2 dτ equal to 1. The cross term vanishes because s and p are orthogonal, so ∫sp dτ = 0.

choices.text: γ is zero for every hybrid
choices.why: γ is zero only for a pure p orbital; for water's bonding hybrids it is 0.5. The cross term vanishes because ∫sp dτ = 0.

choices.text: N is chosen so as to cancel it
choices.why: N is found after the cross term is gone, from N^2 + N^2γ^2 = 1. The term vanishes because s and p are orthogonal.

explanation: s and p are different orbitals of the same atom, so ∫sp dτ = 0, while ∫p^2 dτ = ∫s^2 dτ = 1. That leaves N^2 + N^2γ^2 = 1, so N = 1/√(1 + γ^2).

prompt: The normalized hybrid is N(p + γs), with N = 1/√(1 + γ^2). For water's bonding hybrids, γ = 0.5. What is N? (Give it as a decimal.)
explanation: N = 1/√(1 + 0.5^2) = 1/√1.25 ≈ 1/1.118 ≈ 0.894. Squaring it gives N^2 = 0.80, the p character of these hybrids.

prompt: The s character of a normalized hybrid N(p + γs) is γ^2/(1 + γ^2). For a pure sp^3 hybrid, γ^2 = 1/3. What is its s character, in %?
explanation: (1/3)/(1 + 1/3) = (1/3)/(4/3) = 1/4 = 25%. The rest, 75%, is p character, as expected for sp^3.

prompt: How does the section decide what γ should be for water's bonding hybrids?

choices.text: From the measured bond angle, via cos θ = −γ^2
It assumes perfect sp^3 hybrids, so γ^2 = 1/3
choices.why: That would force the angle to be 109.5°. The section instead works backward from water's measured angle.

choices.text: From the number of lone pairs on the oxygen
choices.why: The lone pairs come into a later estimate. γ for the bonds comes from the measured bond angle through cos θ = −γ^2.

choices.text: It is chosen so that the hybrids are normalized
choices.why: Normalization fixes N for any γ; it doesn't pick γ. The measured bond angle does, through cos θ = −γ^2.

explanation: The geometry comes first: γ is found from the experimentally measured bond angle through cos θ = −γ^2. This equation links the measured structure to the s and p makeup of the hybrids.

prompt: Water's bond angle θ is about 104.5°, and cos 104.5° = −0.25. Using cos θ = −γ^2, what is the mixing coefficient γ of water's bonding hybrids? (Give it as a decimal.)
explanation: −γ^2 = −0.25, so γ^2 = 0.25 and γ = √0.25 = 0.5. This γ gives 1/(1 + 0.25) = 80% p and 20% s character for the bonding hybrids.

prompt: In Example 10.2.1, CO2 is linear, so θ = 180° and cos θ = −1. Using cos θ = −γ^2 and s character = γ^2/(1 + γ^2), what is the s character of the bonding hybrids, in %?
explanation: −γ^2 = −1, so γ^2 = 1, and the s character is 1/(1 + 1) = 1/2 = 50%. The bonding hybrids of CO2 are sp hybrids, (1/√2)(s ± p).

prompt: A set of equivalent bonding hybrids has γ^2 = 0.5. Using cos θ = −γ^2, what is the bond angle θ, in degrees?
explanation: cos θ = −0.5, so θ = 120°. The s character is 0.5/(1 + 0.5) = 1/3, which matches sp^2 hybrids and their 120° angle.

prompt: According to cos θ = −γ^2, how does the s character of a set of bonding hybrids change as the bond angle θ widens from 90° toward 180°?

choices.text: It increases steadily
It decreases steadily
choices.why: Wider angles make cos θ more negative, so γ^2 and the s character grow, not shrink.

choices.text: It stays the same at every angle
choices.why: γ is tied to the angle by cos θ = −γ^2, so changing the angle changes the s character.

choices.text: It rises, then falls back to zero
choices.why: cos θ falls steadily from 0 to −1 over this range, so γ^2, and with it the s character, rises the whole way.

explanation: As θ goes from 90° to 180°, cos θ goes from 0 to −1, so γ^2 rises from 0 to 1 and the s character γ^2/(1 + γ^2) rises from 0 to 50%. Pure p orbitals give 90° and sp hybrids give 180°.

prompt: The section says water's bonding hybrids are better described as sp^4. What does that mean?

choices.text: Each is 20% s and 80% p in character
Each mixes one s orbital with four p orbitals
choices.why: Oxygen has only three p orbitals. sp^4 is shorthand for the mix 1/(4 + 1) = 20% s and 4/(4 + 1) = 80% p.

choices.text: Each is 25% s and 75% p, like sp^3
choices.why: That is perfect sp^3, which fits 109.5°. Water's 104.5° angle gives 20% s and 80% p.

choices.text: Oxygen forms four bonds using these hybrids
choices.why: Oxygen forms two O–H bonds in water. The 4 describes the ratio of p to s character, 80% to 20%.

explanation: With γ = 0.5, the bonding hybrids are 80% p and 20% s, so they are not perfect sp^3 hybrids. Calling them sp^4 does not mean four p orbitals; it means each hybrid is 20% s and 80% p.

prompt: When the p character of all four of oxygen's hybrids in water is added up, why must the total be 3?

choices.text: They are built from three p orbitals
Oxygen forms three bonds in water
choices.why: Oxygen forms two bonds. The total is 3 because the four hybrids are made from three p orbitals (and one s).

choices.text: A water molecule has three atoms
choices.why: The number of atoms doesn't matter. What fixes the total is the three p orbitals on O that go into the hybrids.

choices.text: Oxygen holds three lone pairs in water
choices.why: Oxygen has two lone pairs in water. The total p character equals the number of p orbitals combined, three.

explanation: The four hybrids are made from one 2s and three 2p orbitals, so their p characters must add up to 3. This lets the section estimate the lone-pair p character from 0.8 + 0.8 + x + x = 3.

prompt: Oxygen's three p orbitals give a total p character of 3 over its four hybrids. Each bonding hybrid in water is 0.8 p, and the two lone-pair hybrids are assumed identical, each with p character x. What is x? (Give it as a decimal.)
explanation: 0.8 + 0.8 + x + x = 3, so 2x = 1.4 and x = 0.7. The lone-pair hybrids are 70% p and 30% s, richer in s than the 25% of a perfect sp^3 hybrid.

prompt: How does the estimated angle between water's two lone-pair hybrids compare with the H–O–H bond angle?

choices.text: Larger: about 115° versus 104.5°
Smaller: about 90° versus 104.5°
choices.why: The lone-pair hybrids have more s character than the bonding ones, and more s means a wider angle, about 115°.

choices.text: The same: 109.5° for both
choices.why: Equal angles would need equal s and p character. The lone-pair hybrids (30% s) differ from the bonding ones (20% s).

choices.text: Much larger: 180° versus 104.5°
choices.why: 180° would need γ = 1, 50% s. The lone-pair hybrids are only 30% s, which gives about 115°.

explanation: With 70% p, 1/(1 + γ^2) = 0.7 gives −γ^2 = 1 − 1/0.7 = −0.43, and cos θ = −0.43 gives θ ≈ 115°. The lone pairs spread wider than the O–H bonds, at 104.5°.

prompt: Compared with a perfect sp^3 hybrid, how do water's lone-pair hybrids differ?

choices.text: They have more than 25% s and are held closer to O
They have less than 25% s and point toward the H atoms
choices.why: That describes the bonding hybrids, about 20% s. The lone-pair hybrids, about 30% s, are less directional and held more tightly to O.

choices.text: They are pure p orbitals with no s character
choices.why: The lone-pair hybrids are about 30% s and 70% p, so they contain more s, not none.

choices.text: They have exactly 25% s, like any sp^3 hybrid
choices.why: Water's hybrids are not perfect sp^3. The p characters must total 3, and with 0.8 p in each bond, the lone pairs get 0.7 p, so 30% s.

explanation: The lone-pair hybrids are about 30% s and 70% p, more than the 25% s of a perfect sp^3 hybrid. More s character makes them less directional and holds them more tightly to the oxygen atom.

prompt: Why are the hybrids used in water's O–H bonds more directional than the lone-pair hybrids?

choices.text: They have more p character, 80% versus 70%
They have more s character than the lone pairs
choices.why: It's the reverse: the bonding hybrids are 20% s and the lone-pair hybrids 30% s. It is p character that makes an orbital directional.

choices.text: They contain no s character at all
choices.why: The bonding hybrids are 20% s. They are more directional because they have more p character than the lone-pair hybrids.

choices.text: They hold two electrons rather than one
choices.why: Each bonding hybrid starts half filled, while each lone-pair hybrid holds two. Directionality comes from p character, not electron count.

explanation: An s orbital is spherical and a p orbital is directional. With 80% p, the bonding hybrids are more directional and put their electron density in the bonding region between O and H; the 70% p lone-pair hybrids are less directional.

prompt: What shortcoming of the valence bond description of water does the section's warning point out?

choices.text: It gives both lone pairs the same energy
It predicts a bond angle of exactly 90°
choices.why: With hybrids fitted to the measured angle, the VB picture gives 104.5°. The warning is about the two lone pairs being identical.

choices.text: It cannot describe the O–H bonds at all
choices.why: VB describes the two O–H bonds with hybrid orbitals. The shortcoming concerns the lone pairs, which it makes identical in energy.

choices.text: It puts three lone pairs on oxygen
choices.why: It gives oxygen two lone pairs, correctly. The problem is that both sit in identical hybrids and so have the same energy.

explanation: The valence bond picture puts the two lone pairs in identical hybrid orbitals, so they have the same energy. Photoelectron spectroscopy shows that they do not, which is a shortcoming of applying VB theory to water.
